subChunks.title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE Output
subChunks.hookHtml: Before optimising a slow query, you need to know why it is slow. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows you exactly what the engine did — and what it cost.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Basic EXPLAIN

EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';

Shows the execution plan without running the query. Costs are estimates from the planner.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';

Actually runs the query and shows both estimated and actual costs. Use on development or staging — it executes the query, so avoid on slow destructive queries in production.

Key terms in PostgreSQL EXPLAIN output

Seq Scan on apprentices  (cost=0.00..12.50 rows=100 width=20)
                         (actual time=0.01..0.8 rows=3 loops=1)
  • Seq Scan — full sequential scan (no index used)
  • Index Scan — uses index to find rows, then fetches from table
  • Index Only Scan — satisfied entirely from index (covering index)
  • Bitmap Index Scan — combines multiple indexes
  • cost — estimated (startup cost)..(total cost) in arbitrary planner units
  • rows — estimated row count
  • actual time — real ms (startup..total)
  • loops — how many times this node ran (relevant for nested loops)

Reading a join plan

Hash Join  (cost=...)
  Hash Cond: (a.mentor_id = m.id)
  ->  Seq Scan on apprentices as a
  ->  Hash
        ->  Seq Scan on mentors as m

Read bottom-up: the inner nodes are computed first. Here: mentors is hashed, then apprentices is scanned and each row is probed against the hash.

storyBeats.text: The slow query page shows a 3-second response time. The fix is invisible without seeing the plan.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: EXPLAIN is your oracle. Seq Scan on a million-row table means no index was used — or the planner decided a scan was cheaper. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the actual time alongside the estimate. If the estimate is wildly wrong, run ANALYZE to refresh statistics. Read the plan bottom-up.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Plan interpretation

Read this simplified EXPLAIN ANALYZE output and answer the questions below:

Seq Scan on apprentices (cost=0.00..210.00 rows=8000 width=40)
                        (actual time=0.05..45.2 rows=8000 loops=1)
Filter: ((rank)::text = 'Mage'::text)
Rows Removed by Filter: 992000
  1. Was an index used? How do you know?
  2. How many rows were scanned vs returned?
  3. What would you add to speed this up?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. No index was used — the plan shows 'Seq Scan' (sequential scan). If an index were used, it would show 'Index Scan' or 'Index Only Scan'.

2. 1,000,000 rows were scanned (8000 returned + 992,000 removed by filter). The engine read the entire table and discarded 99.2% of rows.

3. Add an index on rank: CREATE INDEX ON apprentices(rank). With this index, the engine can jump directly to 'Mage' rows without scanning the rest. For a query also selecting name and xp, a covering index (rank, name, xp) would enable an index-only scan.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain the difference between a Seq Scan, an Index Scan, and an Index Only Scan. When would the planner choose each one?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Seq Scan: the engine reads every row in the table in storage order. Used when: (a) there is no relevant index, (b) the query returns a large fraction of the table (making index overhead not worthwhile), or (c) the table is very small.

Index Scan: the engine traverses the B-tree index to find matching row locations, then fetches each row from the main table ('heap'). Used when: the query is selective (few rows match) and there is a relevant index. Has random I/O overhead from heap fetches.

Index Only Scan: the engine satisfies the entire query from the index alone — no heap fetch needed (covering index). Fastest for selective queries when all needed columns are in the index. Requires the index to contain all columns referenced in the query.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what EXPLAIN ANALYZE output tells you and how to identify whether a query is using an index.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
options: EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows real timing
EXPLAIN shows actual costs; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimates
EXPLAIN ANALYZE is available only in PostgreSQL
EXPLAIN runs faster because it does not touch indexes
questions.answer: EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan without running the query; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows real timing
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN is safe to run anytime — it only displays the plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports actual rows and timings alongside the estimates.

questions.prompt: EXPLAIN output shows `Seq Scan on apprentices ... Rows Removed by Filter: 999980`. What does this mean?
options: The engine scanned all ~1M rows and discarded 999,980 — only 20 rows matched. An index on the filter column would dramatically speed this up
20 rows were removed by a bad WHERE clause
Seq Scan is preferred over Index Scan for this query
questions.answer: The engine scanned all ~1M rows and discarded 999,980 — only 20 rows matched. An index on the filter column would dramatically speed this up
questions.explanation: Rows Removed by Filter shows how many rows were read but not returned. High removal on a Seq Scan indicates a full table scan that could be replaced with an index scan, reducing the work from 1M rows to 20.

questions.prompt: The planner estimates 100 rows but EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 50,000 actual rows. What should you do?
options: Run ANALYZE on the table to update statistics so the planner has accurate row count estimates
questions.answer: Run ANALYZE on the table to update statistics so the planner has accurate row count estimates
questions.explanation: The planner relies on table statistics (row counts, column value distributions) to estimate costs. Stale statistics cause bad plan choices. ANALYZE updates statistics. In PostgreSQL, autovacuum runs ANALYZE periodically; you may need to run it manually after bulk loads.

questions.prompt: A Seq Scan on a 200-row table is shown in EXPLAIN. Should you add an index?
options: Probably not — the planner correctly chooses Seq Scan for very small tables where index overhead exceeds the scan cost
Yes — always add an index when Seq Scan appears
Yes — but only if the table will grow later
No — the table must be > 1000 rows before indexes help
questions.answer: Probably not — the planner correctly chooses Seq Scan for very small tables where index overhead exceeds the scan cost
questions.explanation: For tiny tables (dozens to low hundreds of rows), a full scan is faster than an index lookup — the index has overhead (B-tree traversal, random heap fetches). The planner knows this and deliberately chooses Seq Scan. Seq Scan is not always a problem.
